Hi /v/MusicMakers! I'm 19 years old, and I can play a few instruments, but since highschool is over (no more high school band/orchestra) and I don't really have many friends that play music, I need some sort of outlet for my music. I can play the cello, flute, piccolo, guitar and piano. So the question is, what kind of music could I make with just those instruments, a laptop, and a rockband microphone?
What kind of music should I make?

Pop Folk, like Edward Sharp and the Magnetic Zeroes, or Johnny Flynn.

Is your piano a midi controller?
What a coincidence, that is one of my favorite genres. I do have access to a midi controller keyboard. But like... where do I even start?
I would start with a chorus's chord progression on the piano. Maybe 3-4 good chords. Hum a meldody, or write some lyrics. Then break off into your verses and come up with something catchy.
Download a DAW! Watch some youtube tutorials. Get started.
Don't worry so much about genre and just start putting a song together. Get used to the writing and recording process. As you get more used to writing, you'll develop into a genre.

Would you by chance know some good resources to get started on writing music? The way I'd probably go about it is to start playing a basic chord progression on guitar, put it on loop and then record a long improvisation session and pick out the good parts to use as a melody, and hope everything else will just fall into place.

I don't know of any resources. Everyone writes different and I personally think it is better to find your own process.

The way you're talking about writing is pretty similar to how I do it. Sometimes I'll have a basic idea in my head so I make a click track (could be just a metronome click or a very simple drum line) then put down some sort of framework like simple chord progression and build from there. Other times I'll make a bassline or some melody and build off that.

Usually I work in sections. I'll create a part of the song, get to a particular point and then try to decide where I want to take it. What changes I want to include. I used to write all parts to a section (say a chorus) before moving to the next section. Lately I have been stopping myself from doing that and come up with the basic feeling of the section and then move on. Once I get the framework of the entire song done, then I go back and put in all the fiddly bits. I found if I complete a section I'll get stuck because now that one section is all I can hear in my head.

I think the most important thing with writing is experimentation. Play around with new things and push yourself to work outside of your regular genres you'd listen to. You can learn a lot about music that way.

Thanks for the advice! I feel pretty inspired now, so I've already contacted my friend to set up a jam session (he plays bass guitar).

So how should I have the music written? Should it just all be audio recordings, or midi files which are then used as sheet music to make the recordings, or just go old-school handwritten on staff paper?

Again, that is probably going to depend on you.

For me, I use Sonar and usually write the framework of the song in MIDI. This gives me flexibility to shove parts of the song around, duplicate parts, extend or shorten phrases, while being able to listen to the change right away. From there, I can add audio tracks and go crazy. I personally can't read notation, so if I have to go back later and recreate/replay something, I can figure it out with the MIDI note data or just by listening to it.

Do you have any musical friends, or are you wanting to make solo music? Also, to state the obvious (since nobody else has yet), play to your passions. I don't know any pop folk artists (or honestly even what that sound is like), but you mentioned in another comment that you like this genere, so if that floats your boat, start there.

Making music should be fun, enjoy yourself and the rest will follow.

I have a few friends that play music but I don't think they would want to commit enough time to actually create something. Pop folk might be hard for me because I have pretty much no creative writing experience, so I can't really write lyrics, and my singing isn't the greatest (yet). I think I'll start with something more instrumental like Message to Bears.

It's a heavy handed compromise, but probably for the better when you consider the appstore as a whole, so kudos I guess?

I think it's a terrible idea.

With IPv4, it's almost assumed you are behind a NAT, especially for a wireless device. Most home routers don't NAT for IPv6. The NAT added a decent layer of security. Ditching that security, as well as making your packets bigger for a wireless device, just seems stupid. Especially adding intentional delay to that end.

With IPv4, it's almost assumed you are behind a NAT, especially for a wireless device.

And this has caused many problems. ICE / STUN, TURN, UPnP-IGD, NAT-T, and the whole swath of fixes to the problems created by NAT stand as a testament to this

Most home routers don't NAT for IPv6.

That's because NAT was an ugly hack and IPv6 was designed in part to fix the brokenness that necessitated it.

The NAT added a decent layer of security.

Only as an accident, and not one that should be relied upon in place of real security measures

Ditching that security, as well as making your packets bigger for a wireless device, just seems stupid.

The benefits far outweigh the consequences of a slightly larger packet header, and there is less processing the router needs to do (and less state to hold), so the routing is more efficient. And if the device implements a simple soft firewall (as almost all IPv6 compatible SOHO routers seem to be doing nowadays) you're only better off for using the right tool for the job.

NAT does not provide any additional security for IPv6, given that the address used publicly is generated randomly and changed regularly. Firewalling works the same as before, except the absence of NAT reduces the computational overhead.
